newsitem.title: USA: Dollar hits fresh 8-year high vs. mark.
newsitem.headline: Dollar hits fresh 8-year high vs. mark.

text.p: The dollar rose to a fresh eight-year high against the German mark Tuesday after the Bundesbank held official interest rates steady and German officials showed little concern over the dollar's recent climb.

The German central bank surprised investors by fixing its official money market rate at 3 percent for the next two weeks. Some experts had predicted the central bank would let the market push the rate higher.

"The market was anticipating some kind of change in German rates and when it didn't come, people started buying dollars against the mark," said Kisoo Park, senior currency dealer at Bank of Boston. Higher German rates would tend to make German investments more attractive and boost demand for marks.

Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing also boosted the dollar with comments to German weekly magazine Boerse-Online indicating German officials were only worried about the speed of the dollar's ascent, not the dollar's level.
"It seems like the market will try to test whether the Bundesbank will come in and support the mark," said Steen Jakobsen, treasurer at Christiania Bank in New York.

The dollar jumped to 1.8800 marks from 1.8660 late Monday, bringing its rise against the mark this year to 22 percent, with a 7.5 percent rise since June 1. The dollar touched 1.8832 during the session, the highest since October 1989.
The dollar also rose to 119.23 Japanese yen from 118.33 late Monday and to 1.5350 Swiss francs from 1.5250.
The British pound fell to $1.6245 from $1.6314. the dollar rose to Canadian $1.3804 from C$1.3787.
The respected German Ifo economic institute issued a report that a dollar move above 1.90 marks would "set off alarm bells" at the Bundesbank, which temporarily halted the dollar's climb.
But bargain-hunters quickly intervened to push the dollar back up, and traders asserted the Bundesbank has little or no reason to halt the dollar's rise versus the mark.

"The world economy is benefiting from a strong dollar, with Germany first and foremost. It's hard to see why they should fight this trend," said Jakobsen. A stronger dollar makes German exports cheaper in global markets.

The dollar rose in Asian trading after Thailand's central bank suspended operations of 42 finance companies to help ease the current cash crunch stemming from a sharp economic slump. Investors bought dollars against the Thai baht, causing some spillover buying of dollars against the yen, dealers said.
Japan's influential Vice Finance Minister for International Affairs, Eisuke Sakakibara, also lifted the dollar by denying a rumour that he had warned traders not to buy the dollar above 119 yen.
Sakakibara added that he would not comment on foreign exchange market movements.
"Sakakibara doesn't seem to have a problem with the dollar, which helped push it higher," Jakobsen said.
